            Why these numbers?

            Your gut can only absorb so much carbohydrate an hour. One carb type (glucose or maltodextrin) tops out near 60 g/hr; glucose + fructose blends reach about 90 g/hr.

            How to measure it

            Weigh yourself right before and after a ride, in minimal kit and towelled dry. Each pound lost is about 15 oz of sweat (1 kg ≈ 1 L). Add what you drank, then divide by the hours. The Journal's weigh-in does the math.

            Gel rounding

            Whatever the gels don't cover goes into the bottles, to 0.1 g. Rounding down can push bottles over the suggested strength; the app flags it in red.

            A / B / A / B through the ride. Only items of a different form from your main one are listed.
            Why alternate?

            Alternating is for a change of form. A chew or a bite of food between gels breaks up hours of the same sweet texture; a second gel only changes the wrapper, so items of the same form are not listed.

            Our rule

            Switching form does not cost you fuel: in a lab study at 120 g/h, carbs from chews, gels and a drink were used at the same peak rate.

                The science

                What we stand on

                Every number in the calculator stands on one of these beliefs. Tap one to see the evidence.

                Researchstudies and reviews Guidelineposition stands and agencies Our ruleour call, labelled as ours

                13 core beliefs

                Bottles never go above 8% carbsResearch

                What we believe

                A little carbohydrate helps fluid absorb, but stronger drinks slow fluid delivery. So the hotter the day, the weaker the bottle, and 8% is the ceiling.

                Why

                • A small amount of carbohydrate (1–3%) speeds fluid absorption, while drinks at 8% and above delay fluid delivery. Glucose + fructose blends soften that at higher concentrations.

                  GSSI SSE #244, Baker (2023)

                • Fluid delivery was compromised once concentration went above 6%, and adding sodium didn't fix it.

                  Jeukendrup et al., 2009

                • Repeated drinking of an 8% carb beverage during exercise significantly slowed gastric emptying; lower concentrations didn't.

                  Murray et al., IJSNEM 1999

                What the app does

                Hot: 3% (fluid first). Moderate: 6%. Cold: 8%, and the app will not go higher. Our old 10% cold band was a tolerance habit, not evidence.

                Heat cuts how much carb you can useResearch

                What we believe

                In the heat your body burns less of the carbohydrate you take in, and your stomach empties more slowly.

                Why

                • Cyclists at 35°C vs 16°C oxidized less of the carbohydrate they drank and burned 25% more muscle glycogen.

                  Jentjens et al., J Appl Physiol 2002

                • Runners in the heat used ~20% less ingested carbohydrate even with hydration kept normal.

                  Mougin et al., 2025

                • In a 49°C (120°F) room, water left the stomach more slowly than at 18°C, tracking rising core temperature. At 35°C it slowed only when riders were dehydrated.

                  Neufer et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 1989

                What the app does

                The "Heat: lower carb target ~15%" toggle. Off by default; the app nudges you in the Hot band.

                Above 60 g/hr you need glucose + fructoseResearch

                What we believe

                One kind of sugar tops out around 60 g/hr because the gut can only absorb it so fast. Going higher takes a glucose + fructose mix.

                Why

                • A single carbohydrate type tops out around 60 g/hr because its intestinal transporter saturates; glucose + fructose together can push oxidation to ~105 g/hr.

                  Jeukendrup, Eur J Sport Sci 2008

                • ~60 g/hr for 2–3 hr efforts; ~90 g/hr for ultra-endurance, only with multiple transportable carbohydrates.

                  Jeukendrup, Sports Med 2014GSSI SSE #106

                What the app does

                Red warning if a single-source product is used above 60 g/hr. Note above 90 g/hr. The library tags each product's carb type.

                Two sugars beat one, and your gut is trainableResearch

                What we believe

                Glucose and fructose enter through different doors in the gut, so a blend gets more fuel in than either one alone. How much your gut handles can be trained: build up to a high carb target in training, not on race day.

                Why

                • Glucose (and maltodextrin, which is chains of glucose) is absorbed by one transporter that saturates around 60 g/hr. Fructose uses a different one, which is why blends go higher.

                  Jeukendrup, Eur J Sport Sci 2008Jeukendrup, Sports Med 2014

                • Cyclists drinking carbohydrate at a very high rate burned a glucose + fructose drink at a peak of about 1.75 g/min (roughly 105 g/hr), about 65% more than glucose alone (1.06 g/min).

                  Jentjens & Jeukendrup, Br J Nutr 2005

                • A 2:1 glucose:fructose drink improved time-trial performance by 8% over the same amount of glucose alone.

                  Currell & Jeukendrup, MSSE 2008

                • Across 14 studies, fructose + glucose drinks (0.5–1 part fructose per part glucose) gave small to moderate gains in power (1–9%) over glucose alone, and better gut comfort.

                  Rowlands et al., Sports Med 2015

                • The gut adapts. Gastric emptying and stomach comfort can be trained, and how much carbohydrate the gut absorbs follows what you regularly eat.

                  Jeukendrup, Sports Med 2017

                • In races, athletes who took in more carbohydrate reported more nausea and flatulence; in Ironman races they also finished faster.

                  Pfeiffer et al., MSSE 2012

                • Form is about comfort, not fuel: at 120 g/hr, carbohydrate from a drink, gels and chews was burned at the same peak rate.

                  Hearris et al., J Appl Physiol 2022

                • The 10 g/hr trigger, the 2–3 week build-up, the 2-hour line and the nudge toward a second form (in a plan note, and in alternating only between forms) are our rules of thumb, not study findings.

                  Our rule

                What the app does

                Each product can carry the glucose:fructose ratio its label states; it stays blank when the label doesn't say. On a ride of 2 hours or more, when every carb in the plan is one form at one ratio, a note suggests a second form or carb type (not on a No gels day, when you have chosen bottles only). Fine-tune alternates only between different forms. When today's plan is more than 10 g/hr above the most you have logged on a ride, a note suggests stepping up over 2–3 weeks. Both are notes only: the app never changes your numbers for them.

                Age groups, percentiles and PRsOur rule

                What we believe

                A result means more when it's compared fairly: with your own age group, against the share of the field you beat, and only with legs that were raced as advertised.

                Why

                • Age group: IRONMAN and USA Triathlon place you by your age on December 31 of the race year, so your group stays the same all season. Bands are 18–24, then five-year bands (25–29 … 75–79), then 80+.

                  Race rules

                • Percentile is the share of the field you beat: (1 − place ÷ finishers) × 100. 22nd of 180 beats 88% of the age group. Higher is better. Imported spreadsheet percentiles where lower was better are flipped the same way.

                  Our rule

                • Fairness flags keep PRs honest: a current-assisted swim, a short or long leg, or an altered course (like a cancelled swim) is left out of that leg's PR and out of the overall PR for the distance. It can still earn a course best. A wetsuit is not a flag: wetsuit swims count.

                  Our rule

                • Heat-adjusted run: run time is scaled by the dew point, 0% below 60°F, 1% at 60–64, 2% at 65–69, 3.5% at 70–74 and 5% at 75 and up, then compared. The bands are adapted from the athlete's own method: a heuristic, not a published model.

                  Heuristic

                What the app does

                Each race shows its age-group band from your birthday; the Summary has Current age group and All time views. Percentiles and ranks are computed from place and finishers, never stored. Wins lines only use unflagged legs for PRs, need at least two earlier comparable races, and are never negative.

                Drink to your sweat rate, not a weather formulaGuideline

                What we believe

                Every rider sweats differently, so your measured sweat rate beats any formula. The goal is to keep body-water loss under 2%.

                Why

                • ACSM: drink to keep body-water loss under 2%, typically 400–800 mL/hr depending on sweat rate and size, with sodium around 0.5–0.7 g per liter. Sweat rates vary so much that a measured sweat test beats any formula.

                  ACSM Position Stand, 2007

                • For events over ~4 hr, replace 50–80% of the sodium you lose in sweat.

                  McCubbin, via CTS

                • Warmer air raises sweat rate about 0.04 L/hr per °C. Outdoor prediction also needs sun, wind, humidity, speed and body size, and is still only about ±0.45 L/hr, so weighing yourself on your own rides is sharper.

                  Exp Physiol 2023J Appl Physiol 2024

                What the app does

                Fluid checks at 0.4 / 0.8 / 1.2 L/hr. A sweat-rate field in Settings, not a weather formula. "Feels-like" temperature is the one weather input because your weather app already folds in humidity and wind.

                Sodium follows sweatResearch

                What we believe

                Sweat saltiness is personal. Your hourly sodium loss is that saltiness times how much you sweat, so it rises when you sweat more.

                Why

                • Sweat sodium concentration is an individual trait (roughly 200–2,000 mg/L; ~1,000 is typical) and is what a sweat test reports. Hourly loss is that concentration times sweat volume, so it rises with heat, and concentration itself creeps up at higher sweat rates as ducts reabsorb less.

                  Baker, 2017

                What the app does

                Settings stores mg/L; the plan multiplies by today's fluid, so a Hot-day fluid bump raises the sodium target with it. Drinking more plain water at a fixed sodium intake is the recipe for dilutional hyponatremia.

                Heat stress is WBGT, not feels-likeGuideline

                What we believe

                Heat stress depends on sun, wind and humidity as well as air temperature. WBGT counts all of them; the heat index assumes shade.

                Why

                • Wet bulb globe temperature is the heat-stress index used by ACSM, OSHA, the U.S. military and NWS. It combines temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation; the heat index assumes shade.

                  NWS Tulsa: WBGTNWS: WBGT vs heat index

                • Our estimate uses the same method as NWS's national WBGT forecast: the Dimiceli–Piltz black-globe equation with the Hunter–Minyard natural wet bulb, fed by Open-Meteo's hourly temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation.

                  NDFD WBGT algorithm (Boyer, NWS/MDL)

                • For U.S. locations the app first asks NWS for its own operational WBGT forecast (an NDFD element since June 2022) and uses that; elsewhere, or if NWS doesn't answer, it estimates with the same method. The finding says which one you got.

                  NWS Service Change Notice 22-43

                What the app does

                When you use the weather lookup, the concentration band is set by average WBGT over your ride window (defaults: Hot ≥ 80°F, Cold < 60°F WBGT). Typed temperatures still use the feels-like thresholds. It's a forecast-based estimate, not a globe thermometer; shade, pavement and local wind move the real number.

                Caffeine goes where it works: the back halfResearch

                What we believe

                Caffeine should be peaking when fatigue sets in. On a long ride, that's the back half.

                Why

                • The ISSN position stand: 3–6 mg/kg taken about 60 minutes before it is needed improves endurance performance; doses above ~9 mg/kg add side effects, not benefit.

                  Guest et al., 2021

                • Plasma caffeine peaks 30–60 minutes after a dose and has a half-life of roughly 5 hours, so a dose in the first hour still works in hour four but is fading. Late-exercise doses restore performance when fatigue sets in.

                  Cox et al., 2002

                What the app does

                Caffeine gels get their own times, shown as “C at 2:30” under their hour. They are spread evenly from your “Caffeine from” time (Plan › Advanced; on Auto, the first gel on rides of 2.5 h or less, else 2.5 h before the finish but no later than 1:30 in) to 60 minutes before the finish, never later, on the half hour where the window allows, at least 45 minutes apart: one dose for every 2.5 h of that window, within your per-ride limit and none after your cutoff time. A dose that doesn't fit is left out and the Details say why. Each counts in its hour's gels. The app never adds caffeine unless it is switched on in Settings, and never adjusts carbs or sodium for it.

                Small and often beats big gulpsResearch

                What we believe

                Small, regular drinks keep fluid and fuel moving through your stomach. Big gulps of strong drink slow it down.

                Why

                • Serial small drinks empty steadily; big boluses of strong solution do not.

                  NASEM review

                What the app does

                Each bottle gets one number: when to start it, where the one before runs out on your fluid for each hour's forecast (a start within 5 minutes of a whole hour goes on the hour). Its strength is set for its stretch of the ride, never above your strength limit. Gels are whole numbers per hour of the ride: eat a plain gel any time in its hour, and let your bike computer remind you (an Eat alert every 60 minutes on a Garmin Edge). Each hour aims within 5 g of your carbs per hour, as close as whole gels and the strength limit allow; no gel in the last 30 minutes. The exact minutes are in During the ride if you want them. The minimum of 1 gel per hour is practice, not a paper.

                Medications get a flag, never a number changeGuideline

                What we believe

                Some common medications make heat harder to handle, but there's no evidence for a specific fueling change for any one drug.

                Why

                • Clinician guidance groups heat-sensitizing drugs by mechanism: SSRIs/SNRIs (impaired central thermoregulation, more sweating, dehydration and electrolyte risk), tricyclics and antipsychotics (reduced sweating), ADHD stimulants (more heat production), beta blockers (impaired skin blood flow), ACE inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists (blunted thirst), diuretics and lithium (fluid and electrolyte loss), first-generation antihistamines (reduced sweating).

                  Americares / Harvard C-CHANGE provider guideNYC Health: Heat and MedicationsDrug Topics summary

                • The drug-name lookup uses the consolidated list from the Arizona Heat Preparedness Network's Heat and Medications sheet for providers (ADHS, Pima County, UArizona), which draws on CDC's clinician guidance.

                  CDC: Heat and Medications — Guidance for Clinicians

                • We found no study that gives a specific fueling adjustment for any drug, so the app flags the mechanism and never changes a number.

                  Our rule

                What the app does

                The app flags the mechanism and what to watch; it never changes a number because of a medication. Talk to your prescriber about training in heat.

                Where the evidence runs out, we say soOur rule

                What we believe

                Some numbers in the app are our judgment call, not a finding. We'd rather tell you than dress them up.

                Why

                • The exact temperature breakpoints (85°F, 65°F) are ours. Whether 8% is fine for you on a cold day is your gut. Per-person sodium needs vary several-fold.

                • Bottle roles are our call too: splitting fluid by cage count, and the warning when an electrolyte bottle passes ~1,500 mg sodium per liter. We found no study that sets how salty a bottle drunk with gels can be; the concern that a very salty drink plus a gel makes the gut contents hypertonic is reasoning, not a measured limit.

                What the app does

                Anything tagged Our rule is practice, not a paper. Use the journal to find what works for you.

                Coach's guidance: 75–85 g/hrOur rule

                What we believe

                Aim for 75 g/hr on easy rides and 85 g/hr on long rides with intervals.

                Why

                • Our coaching rule: don't plan below 75 — the difference in recovery and how you feel is real.

                What the app does

                The intensity presets start at 75, 85 and 90 g/hr; you can change them in Settings.

                Training volume and the off-seasonGuideline

                What we believe

                fred is a reference, not a coach. The Volume tab shows your hours from Strava and what published guidance says, and it never tells you what to do.

                Why

                • Setting annual hours: look at how much you trained last season; if you managed that volume successfully and easily, you may be able to add 10–15%.

                  Friel, Preparing for the 2010 Season, Part 3

                • The Transition period: usually 2–6 weeks of rest and rejuvenation, starting with a few days fully off. Complete rest isn’t the idea; easy exercise and cross-training keep you moving.

                  Friel, The Transition Period (TrainingPeaks)Friel, Training and the Transition Period

                • Letting fitness fade: Friel suggests losing at least about 20% of fitness in the Transition period; more for athletes who have trained hard for years, less after an easy season.

                  Friel, Lessons from the 2010 Season, Part 2

                How fred calculates

                • Hours are Strava’s moving time (elapsed time for activities you added by hand), for the sports you count.

                • On pace = hours so far ÷ days so far × days in the season.

                • The permission line = (goal − hours so far) ÷ weeks left. In the off-season: the lowest weekly hours for the rest of the off-season that still leaves the rest of next season needing no more than your best 12-week block, rounded up to 0.5 h.

                • Best 12-week block = your most hours in any 84 days in a row last season, ÷ 12.

                • Fitness is a 42-day exponentially weighted average of your daily hours: a time-only version of TrainingPeaks’ Fitness (CTL). It counts hours, not intensity. Fade = 1 − today ÷ the highest value in the last 16 weeks of the season.

                Our rulefred’s math, labelled as ours
                The aero estimate (CdA) from race averagesOur rule

                What we believe

                Your average power, speed and a few answers about weight, tires and road give a fair estimate of your drag area (CdA): useful for comparing your own races, not a wind-tunnel number.

                Why

                • On a steady ride, the power at the pedals goes to drivetrain losses, rolling resistance, climbing and air. On a loop course the climbing comes back on the descents, so what is left after rolling resistance is air drag, which grows with the cube of speed.

                • Rolling resistance is the uncertain part: a 0.001 change in the rolling coefficient moves CdA by about 0.016 at 70.3 speeds. That is why fred asks about tires and road, and why every estimate comes with a range.

                How fred calculates

                • Mass = you + bike + what you carried (bottles, gels, a 1 lb flat kit). Speed = bike distance ÷ bike time. Drivetrain efficiency 0.975. Average power, not normalized power.

                • Air density from the race-hour temperature, humidity and air pressure (Open-Meteo's surface pressure, or your altitude through the standard barometric formula; sea level when neither is known).

                • Rolling coefficient (fred's assumptions): race tubeless or latex 0.0032, race tire with a butyl tube 0.0040, training tire 0.0050; 25 mm +0.0002, 28 mm 0, 30 mm or wider −0.0001; smooth road × 0.9, average × 1.0, rough or chip seal × 1.25.

                • CdA = (0.975 × power − rolling × mass × g × speed) ÷ (½ × air density × speed³). Range: rolling ± 0.0007 and power ± 2%; 50% wider when the estimate is Rough.

                • Quality: Good = a power meter, no more than 15 ft of climbing a mile, wind 12 mph or less. Rough = up to 25 ft a mile and 18 mph (and when wind, climbing or altitude is unknown). Otherwise Not reliable, never counted as a best.

                • From Strava ride data: steady stretches of at least 60 s (flat, even speed and power, no coasting), each with climbing and speed changes taken out; the middle value, with the spread of the middle half as the range.

                Our rulefred’s math, labelled as ours

                Disclaimer

                fred is a planning tool, not medical advice. The numbers come from published sports-nutrition research (see the beliefs above) and from product labels you or we entered; your tolerance for carbs, fluid and sodium is individual and is yours to test in training before racing. Brands reformulate — check the label. If you have a medical condition affecting hydration, electrolytes or blood sugar, talk to a clinician.

                About

                fred is free. Nothing leaves your device: your products and journal are saved in this browser only. Use Download a backup in Settings to keep a copy. On iPhone, add this page to your Home Screen so it behaves like an app and keeps its data.

                Made by Bluebird Multisport

                Privacy note

                Your data, in plain words

                Nothing leaves this device until you sign in with Google. After that:

                What’s stored

                Your Google name, email and photo; settings, closet, bikes and product library; your last plan; your Journal and Races; birthday and gender, if given.

                Where

                Google Firebase (Cloud Firestore), in the United States. Each signed-in device keeps a copy too.

                Who can see it

                Only you: the database’s security rules let an account read and write only its own records. No ads, no analytics, nothing sold.

                Never stored

                Your location history, or health records you didn’t type. The forecast keeps only your last few place names.

                My stack and barcodes

                Your stack is kept with your settings, for you only, never sent to any AI. A scan sends only the barcode number to public label databases (NIH, openFDA, Open Food Facts, USDA).

                Strava (only if you connect it)

                fred keeps a summary of each Strava activity (date, sport, time, distance, climbing, averages) to count your training hours. Your Strava sign-in keys stay on fred’s small server and never reach your browser. Strava data is shown only to you, while you’re signed in, and is never sent to any AI model or other service. For a tighter aero estimate, fred reads that one ride once, on your device, and keeps only the result. Disconnect deletes fred’s copy; so does deleting your account. It isn’t part of Download a backup.

                Imported training history is stored the same way, shown only to you, and part of Download a backup.

                Your TrainingPeaks plan link stays on fred’s server; Remove deletes it.
